Ministry o f Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 161-169
Report on the Glaciological Studies Carried out  
during XXIII Indian Antarctic Expedition
Amit D harw adkar1 , R. Ravindra2 , D. Jayapaul1 , S. Jayaram 3 , P.R. Golani4  
and V. Ravikant5

9 DECEMBER 2003
Antarctic Glaciers Speed Up: Scientists at NSIDC have found that 
glaciers around the area of the Larsen B Ice Shelf accelerated immediately 
after it collapsed early in 2002. (NSIDC)
1  DECEMBER 2003
Ice Shelf Feels the Heat: “Warming waters may doom the Antarctic 
Peninsula’s Larsen Ice Shelf, and other Antarctic ice shelves could be more 
endangered than had been thought, according to a paper published in the 31 
October issue of Science.” NSIDC researcher Ted Scambos is quoted in 
the paper. (Science Magazine)
6 OCTOBER 2003
Huge Antarctic iceberg makes a big splash on sea life (EurekAlert)
22-24 SEPTEMBER 2003
Giant Arctic ice shelf splits: Largest Arctic ice shelf breaks up, freeing 
all water from the freshwater lake it dammed. (ABC Science Online, BBC 
News, Belfast Telegraph, CBC North, CBS News, CNN, CTV, Discovery 
Channel, Edmonton Journal, Edmonton

162 Amit Dharwadkar et al.
Above headlines illustrate that the possibility of global climate change 
and its effects have caught the attention of both the scientific community 
and the public. Several GCMs[Global Climate Model] in vogue predict that 
the global warming has effected a higher degree of melting of glaciers 
(particularly in the polar regions). This contributes to a rise in sea level 
changes which can have drastic effects in low lying coastal areas around 
the world. The polar ice-sheet is a critical component of the GCM and our 
understanding of the growth and movement of Antarctic ice is vital for 
testing the GCMs as well as predictions for the future.
This paper presents an account of glaciological studies carried out 
during the austral summer of 2003-04 in continuation of the work done by 
GSI since the 2n d  Indian Antarctic Expedition. The glaciological studies 
carried out during the 23r d  IAE can be categorized as follows:
1. Iceberg monitoring.
2. Fluctuations in the Polar Ice front.
3. Accumulation/ablation studies on ice-shelf.
ICEBERG MONITORING
Icebergs have their origin in the cliffs of Antarctica’s coast line and 
form some of the most spectacular sights in the world. These icebergs float 
over the sea surface and move along with the prevalent ocean currents in 
the southern seas. These can measure up to several hundred meters in 
length and present a significant hazard to navigation.
Iceberg monitoring was taken up on board the ship MV Emerald Sea 
during the onward and return journey to/from Antarctica. The icebergs 
encountered were systematically recorded using the standard format of 
iceberg monitoring devised by the Norwegian Polar Institute. During the 
onward journey, the first iceberg was sighted at Lat 44°97'S and long 12°51E. 
It is generally observed that the first iceberg sighting has shifted northwards 
with time [Fig-1]. This may be related to the higher instance of iceberg 
formation in recent times. A total o f207 icebergs of various sizes and shapes 
were recorded between Lat 44°47'S and 69°29'S during the onward journey.
During return voyage a total of 128 icebergs were sighted between 
69°36'S and 55°07'S. Fig. 2(a) shows the distribution of the icebergs with 
respect to latitude and size during onward journey while Fig. 2(b) shows 
corresponding distribution during return journey. It can be seen that during 
the onward journey, maximum concentration of icebergs occurs in a zone

between 52°S and 59°S latitudes. During the return journey (late March 
2004), the icebergs are concentrated in two distinct zones ie: 67°-66°S and 
62°-55°S; with iceberg free zone in between. The size distribution of the ice 
bergs points toward a skewed distribution where most of the icebergs sighted 
fall in the range of 500-100m. It is also generally observed that away from 
the continent, the icebergs are mostly of irregular shape and often tilted a 
feature resulting due to sculpturing by wind and waves. Nearer to the coast 
line, the icebergs are usually larger and tabular in shape.
FLUCTUATIONS IN THE POLAR ICE FRONT
The snout of a glacial tongue (“Dakshin Gangotri ” Glacier) overflowing 
the Schirmacher Oasis is being monitored by GSI since more than two 
decades. It has been observed that the snout is retreating at an average 
annual rate of 0.7m. This amounts to a 14m retreat during two decades.
